summary.text: Writing $n=5k+r$, the proof establishes from the fourth-order recurrence and Fibonacci addition identities that $a(5k+r)$ is respectively $(-1)^kF_{5k}$, $(-1)^kF_{5k+1}$, $(-1)^kF_{5k+1}$, $0$, or $(-1)^{k+1}F_{5k+3}$ for $r=0,1,2,3,4$. Taking absolute values removes the alternating signs, while the zero case is $F_0$.

full_proof.text:
Let \(F_m\) denote the Fibonacci numbers, normalized by
\[
F_0=0,\qquad F_1=1,\qquad F_{m+2}=F_{m+1}+F_m.
\]
The sequence in question is the integer sequence \((a_n)_{n\geq 0}\) determined by
\[
a_0=0,\qquad a_1=1,\qquad a_2=1,\qquad a_3=0
\]
and, for every \(m\geq 0\),
\[
a_{m+4}=3a_{m+3}-4a_{m+2}+2a_{m+1}-a_m. \tag{1}
\]
We will obtain an explicit formula for \(a_n\), organized according to the residue of \(n\) modulo \(5\), and then take absolute values.

Define a sign
\[
\varepsilon_k=\begin{cases}
1,&k\text{ even},\\
-1,&k\text{ odd}.
\end{cases}
\]
Thus \(\varepsilon_{k+1}=-\varepsilon_k\) for every \(k\).

We first record the Fibonacci identities that will be used to check the recurrence. Repeated application of the Fibonacci recurrence gives, for every \(j\geq 0\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
F_{j+2}&=F_{j+1}+F_j,\\
F_{j+3}&=F_{j+2}+F_{j+1}=2F_{j+1}+F_j,\\
F_{j+4}&=F_{j+3}+F_{j+2}=3F_{j+1}+2F_j,\\
F_{j+5}&=F_{j+4}+F_{j+3}=5F_{j+1}+3F_j,\\
F_{j+6}&=F_{j+5}+F_{j+4}=8F_{j+1}+5F_j.
\end{aligned} \tag{2}
\]
In particular, the following five relations hold:
\[
F_{j+3}-2F_{j+1}-F_j=0, \tag{3}
\]
\[
F_{j+5}-3F_{j+3}+F_{j+1}=0, \tag{4}
\]
\[
F_{j+6}-3F_{j+5}+4F_{j+3}-F_{j+1}=0, \tag{5}
\]
\[
2F_{j+6}-4F_{j+5}+2F_{j+3}=0, \tag{6}
\]
and
\[
F_{j+6}-2F_{j+5}+F_{j+3}=0. \tag{7}
\]
Indeed, (3) is the formula for \(F_{j+3}\) in (2). For (4), substituting the expressions in (2) gives
\[
(5F_{j+1}+3F_j)-3(2F_{j+1}+F_j)+F_{j+1}=0.
\]
For (5), substitution gives
\[
(8F_{j+1}+5F_j)-3(5F_{j+1}+3F_j)
 +4(2F_{j+1}+F_j)-F_{j+1}=0.
\]
For (6), it gives
\[
2(8F_{j+1}+5F_j)-4(5F_{j+1}+3F_j)
 +2(2F_{j+1}+F_j)=0.
\]
Finally, for (7), it gives
\[
(8F_{j+1}+5F_j)-2(5F_{j+1}+3F_j)
 +(2F_{j+1}+F_j)=0.
\]

Now define an auxiliary sequence \((b_n)\) block by block. For every \(k\geq 0\), set
\[
\begin{aligned}
b_{5k}&=\varepsilon_k F_{5k},\\
b_{5k+1}&=\varepsilon_k F_{5k+1},\\
b_{5k+2}&=\varepsilon_k F_{5k+1},\\
b_{5k+3}&=0,\\
b_{5k+4}&=-\varepsilon_k F_{5k+3}.
\end{aligned} \tag{8}
\]
Every nonnegative integer has exactly one form \(5k+r\) with \(0\leq r<5\), so this defines \(b_n\) for every \(n\).

We claim that \(b_n\) satisfies the same fourth-order recurrence as \(a_n\):
\[
b_{m+4}=3b_{m+3}-4b_{m+2}+2b_{m+1}-b_m. \tag{9}
\]
To prove this, write \(m=5k+r\), where \(r\in\{0,1,2,3,4\}\), and put \(j=5k\) and \(s=\varepsilon_k\). The next block has sign
\(\varepsilon_{k+1}=-s\). We check all five possibilities for \(r\).

If \(r=0\), then the five terms beginning at \(m=j\) are
\[
b_j=sF_j,\quad b_{j+1}=sF_{j+1},\quad
b_{j+2}=sF_{j+1},\quad b_{j+3}=0,\quad
b_{j+4}=-sF_{j+3}.
\]
The right-hand side of (9) is therefore
\[
3\cdot0-4sF_{j+1}+2sF_{j+1}-sF_j
=-s(2F_{j+1}+F_j)=-sF_{j+3},
\]
where the last equality is (3). This is exactly \(b_{j+4}\).

If \(r=1\), the desired new term is the first term in the next block:
\[
b_{j+5}=\varepsilon_{k+1}F_{j+5}=-sF_{j+5}.
\]
The four preceding terms are
\[
b_{j+1}=sF_{j+1},\quad b_{j+2}=sF_{j+1},
\quad b_{j+3}=0,\quad b_{j+4}=-sF_{j+3}.
\]
Hence the recurrence’s right-hand side equals
\[
3(-sF_{j+3})-4\cdot0+2sF_{j+1}-sF_{j+1}
=-3sF_{j+3}+sF_{j+1}.
\]
Identity (4) says \(F_{j+5}=3F_{j+3}-F_{j+1}\), so this is
\(-sF_{j+5}=b_{j+5}\).

If \(r=2\), the desired term is
\[
b_{j+6}=\varepsilon_{k+1}F_{j+6}=-sF_{j+6}.
\]
Using
\[
b_{j+2}=sF_{j+1},\quad b_{j+3}=0,\quad
b_{j+4}=-sF_{j+3},\quad b_{j+5}=-sF_{j+5},
\]
the right-hand side of (9) is
\[
3(-sF_{j+5})-4(-sF_{j+3})+2\cdot0-sF_{j+1}
=s(-3F_{j+5}+4F_{j+3}-F_{j+1}).
\]
By (5), the expression in parentheses is \(-F_{j+6}\), so the result is
\(-sF_{j+6}=b_{j+6}\).

If \(r=3\), then both \(j+6\) and \(j+7\) have the repeated value prescribed at residues \(1\) and \(2\) of the next block, so
\[
b_{j+7}=-sF_{j+6}.
\]
The relevant preceding values are
\[
b_{j+3}=0,\quad b_{j+4}=-sF_{j+3},\quad
b_{j+5}=-sF_{j+5},\quad b_{j+6}=-sF_{j+6}.
\]
Thus the right-hand side of (9) is
\[
3(-sF_{j+6})-4(-sF_{j+5})+2(-sF_{j+3})-0
=s(-3F_{j+6}+4F_{j+5}-2F_{j+3}).
\]
Relation (6), after division by \(2\), says
\(F_{j+6}-2F_{j+5}+F_{j+3}=0\), or equivalently
\[
-3F_{j+6}+4F_{j+5}-2F_{j+3}=-F_{j+6}.
\]
Consequently the displayed recurrence value is
\(-sF_{j+6}=b_{j+7}\), as required.

Finally, suppose \(r=4\). The desired term is at residue \(3\) in the next block, so
\[
b_{j+8}=0.
\]
The preceding terms are
\[
b_{j+4}=-sF_{j+3},\quad b_{j+5}=-sF_{j+5},
\quad b_{j+6}=-sF_{j+6},\quad b_{j+7}=-sF_{j+6}.
\]
The right-hand side of (9) becomes
\[
3(-sF_{j+6})-4(-sF_{j+6})+2(-sF_{j+5})-(-sF_{j+3})
=s(F_{j+6}-2F_{j+5}+F_{j+3}),
\]
which is \(0\) by (7). This agrees with \(b_{j+8}\). Thus all five residue classes have been checked, proving (9).

We next compare the initial values of \(b_n\) with those of \(a_n\). Since \(\varepsilon_0=1\), formula (8) gives
\[
b_0=F_0=0,\qquad b_1=F_1=1,\qquad
b_2=F_1=1,\qquad b_3=0.
\]
Thus \(a_n\) and \(b_n\) have the same first four values, and both satisfy the same recurrence (1)/(9). It follows by induction that
\[
a_n=b_n\qquad\text{for every }n\geq0. \tag{10}
\]
For completeness, in the induction step, once equality is known at indices
\(m,m+1,m+2,m+3\), applying the two recurrences gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_{m+4}
&=3a_{m+3}-4a_{m+2}+2a_{m+1}-a_m\\
&=3b_{m+3}-4b_{m+2}+2b_{m+1}-b_m
=b_{m+4}.
\end{aligned}
\]
Together with the four initial equalities, this proves (10).

It remains to take absolute values. Fix \(n\geq0\), and write
\[
n=5q+r,\qquad 0\leq r<5.
\]
Because \(\varepsilon_q\) is either \(1\) or \(-1\), multiplying a nonnegative integer by \(\varepsilon_q\), or by \(-\varepsilon_q\), does not change its absolute value. Formula (8) and (10) now give the answer case by case:

* If \(r=0\), then
  \[
  |a_n|=|\varepsilon_qF_{5q}|=F_{5q}.
  \]
  Thus one may take the Fibonacci index \(m=5q\).

* If \(r=1\), then
  \[
  |a_n|=|\varepsilon_qF_{5q+1}|=F_{5q+1},
  \]
  so take \(m=5q+1\).

* If \(r=2\), then
  \[
  |a_n|=|\varepsilon_qF_{5q+1}|=F_{5q+1},
  \]
  so again take \(m=5q+1\).

* If \(r=3\), then \(a_n=0=F_0\), so take \(m=0\).

* If \(r=4\), then
  \[
  |a_n|=|-\varepsilon_qF_{5q+3}|=F_{5q+3},
  \]
  so take \(m=5q+3\).

In every case there is a nonnegative integer \(m\) for which
\[
|a_n|=F_m.
\]
Therefore the absolute value of every term of A103311 is a Fibonacci number.
